recentItems.title: Russia says Ukraine launched biggest drone attack on Moscow this year
recentItems.description:
Moscow's mayor says Russian forces have repelled the biggest Ukrainian attack on the city so far this year, with about 450 drones shot down across the Moscow region and more than 1,100 drones downed nationwide, according to the Defence Ministry. 
At least two people were killed and 20 injured, including children, while several fires broke out after the attack on the capital. An oil refinery in the Kapotnya district was hit, while a warehouse and a block of flats were damaged in another district, and more than 400 people, including many children, were moved to safety. 
The strikes came on the final day of voting in Russia's parliamentary elections, with millions voting for 450 seats in the lower house, while a cyberattack reportedly hit Moscow's online voting system. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the attack, pointing to Ukraine's expanding arsenal of homegrown long-range weapons, and said he would accept a de-escalation deal if the political will is there. 

Al Jazeera Dmitry Medvedenko in Moscow and Rory Challands in Kyiv report on the latest developments.

recentItems.title: Iranian schoolgirls compete in robot football at Tehran's RoboCup
recentItems.description:
Hundreds of teams are competing at the RoboCup Iran Open in Tehran, where students are putting their robots to the test across dozens of robotics disciplines. More than 400 teams are taking part in the competition, which aims to develop young people's interest in robotics and artificial intelligence. Among them are Iranian schoolgirls hoping to challenge expectations and pursue careers in the field. Fifteen-year-old Elina Rezvanian said she wants to study robotics at university and compete internationally. Competitors are programming robots to use sensors, cameras and image-processing algorithms to detect and respond to a football. Fourteen-year-old Avina Maleki said she wants to improve her programming skills, create innovative robots and encourage more girls to take part in robotics competitions. For the students, the event is not only about winning matches but developing skills that could shape their future in technology.

Al Jazeera’s Cara Legg reports.

recentItems.title: Saudi Arabia says it intercepted Houthi missile targeting Riyadh
recentItems.description:
Saudi air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh at dawn on Saturday, according to the Saudi-led coalition, which also said attempts to target civilians and civilian infrastructure in Bisha, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu were thwarted. The interception came after Saudi Arabia issued emergency alerts across the kingdom, with residents in Riyadh reporting an explosion and a large plume of black smoke near King Khalid International Airport. Saudi authorities reported no casualties or damage. The Houthis said they had attacked “sensitive” sites in Riyadh and an Aramco facility in Yanbu using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones, but those claims could not be independently verified. The latest escalation follows weeks of renewed fighting between Saudi-backed forces and the Houthis, with clashes also intensifying in several parts of Yemen. 

Al Jazeera's Yousef Mawry reports from Sanaa.

recentItems.title: Cape Town's plan to cage its baboons sparks fierce backlash
recentItems.description:
Many see baboons as an iconic, playful part of Cape Town's wild landscape, but others view them as pests that raid bins, climb onto roofs, and enter people's homes. Now the city wants to permanently enclose about 60 of them, targeting two troops on the Cape Peninsula, a proposal that has triggered angry protests.

Simon's Town resident Sue-Anne Norton says the baboons are wild animals that should not be caged or fenced in, warning some could kill themselves trying to escape. The city argues the animals have become increasingly dependent on urban areas, creating conflict with residents and compromising their own welfare. 

Officials say relocating them to another wild environment was considered but would be ecologically damaging, leaving a purpose-built urban wildlife centre as the alternative.

Al Jazeera's Lou Browne reports.

recentItems.title: How much of a challenge are recurrent bombings to Pakistan? | Inside Story
recentItems.description:
Another Friday prayer, another attack on a mosque, this time in northwestern Pakistan.

An armed group linked to Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan -- the Pakistani Taliban -- has claimed responsibility.

Attacks like this have happened for around 20 years. Pakistan's government says many of them are launched from Afghanistan, just across the border. And relations between the two countries have soured.

So, how should Islamabad deal with this threat?

Presenter Rob Matheson discusses with Hassan Khan, a political and security affairs analyst, Victoria Jones, senior research fellow at the Asia-Pacific Foundation, and Sahar Khan, non-resident fellow at the Institute for Global Affairs.
